name: HyperGraphRAG

paper.title: HyperGraphRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Hypergraph-Structured Knowledge Representation

construction.unit: n-ary fact: one hyperedge sentence plus the entities it connects
construction.kept_as: chunks verbatim; LLM-extracted hyperedge sentences and entity descriptions
construction.processing: documents cut into 1,200-token chunks (100 overlap); one LLM prompt splits each chunk into knowledge segments (hyperedges, completeness score 0-10) and lists each segment's entities (name, type, description, importance 0-100); up to 2 extra gleaning passes

organization.structure: knowledge hypergraph stored as a bipartite graph: entity nodes and hyperedge nodes, an edge for each membership
organization.stores: NetworkX graph + three NanoVectorDB stores (entities, hyperedges, chunks) + chunk text store
organization.index: text-embedding-3-small over entity name + description and over hyperedge sentences; chunk vectors are built but not queried

management.operations: new documents are chunked and extracted into the same graph; entities with the same (upper-cased) name are merged, their descriptions joined and LLM-summarised past 500 tokens; identical hyperedge sentences merge with summed scores

retrieval.query: the construction prompt is run on the question: its entity names form the entity query and its extracted sentences form the hyperedge query (code)
retrieval.candidates: top 60 entities and top 60 hyperedges by cosine similarity (> 0.2)
retrieval.selection: one-hop expansion in the bipartite graph (entities to their hyperedges, hyperedges to their entities) plus the source chunks of both; each list cut at 4,000 tokens
retrieval.budget: about 9.2k retrieved tokens at k = 60 (Medicine, Fig. 6a)

use.context: three CSV tables (entities, hyperedges, source chunks) merged from both routes, inside a unified prompt
use.reasoning: single GPT-4o-mini call: reasoning in <think>, answer in <answer>

classify.note: The hypergraph is stored as an ordinary bipartite graph. Candidates come from dense search; the graph only adds one-hop neighbours. Management is 'consolidate' because same-name entities are merged and long descriptions LLM-summarised (inherited LightRAG code); nothing is deleted or edited otherwise.

stages.ingestion: Domain documents (for example the 2024 ESC hypertension guideline, 179k tokens) are cut into 1,200-token chunks with 100 tokens of overlap.
stages.construction: An LLM rewrites each chunk as a list of knowledge segments, each one sentence with a completeness score, and names the entities in each segment with type, description and importance score.
stages.organization: Each segment becomes a hyperedge node linked to its entities in a bipartite graph; entities and hyperedges are embedded in separate vector stores.
stages.update: New documents are added to the same graph; entities with the same name are merged and their descriptions summarised when long.
stages.retrieval: Entities and hyperedges are matched to the question by vector similarity (top 60 each); retrieved entities pull in their hyperedges, retrieved hyperedges pull in their entities, and both pull in the chunks they came from.
stages.answer: The generator reads entity, hyperedge and chunk tables and answers after a reasoning block.

summary: Replaces the binary triples of graph RAG with n-ary facts: each LLM-extracted sentence becomes a hyperedge over all its entities, and entities and hyperedges are retrieved by vector search and expanded to their neighbours and source chunks.

headline: A memory item is an LLM-written sentence (hyperedge) tied to every entity it mentions, not a (subject, relation, object) triple; the source chunk stays attached.
Retrieval is plain vector search over entities and over hyperedges (top 60 each), then one hop in the bipartite graph; there is no graph walk or reranker.
In the code the question is run through the same extraction prompt as the corpus, and the paper's score weighting, thresholds and separate chunk search are not implemented.

open_questions: The question sets are built by the authors from 1-3 hop samples of 'knowledge fragments'; the paper does not say which graph the hops were taken over, and the datasets are only on Terabox.

No run compares hyperedges with binary triples inside the same pipeline, so the n-ary representation and the rest of the pipeline (LLM query rewriting, 4,000-token tables, chunk attachment) are not separated.
Results are single runs at temperature 1.0 with no variance reported.

glance.a: A hyperedge: one LLM-written sentence stating a fact, linked to every entity it mentions (name, type, description), plus the chunk it came from.
The chunk is kept verbatim; hyperedges and entity descriptions are LLM rewrites, and long merged descriptions are summarised.
A bipartite graph of entity nodes and hyperedge nodes, with separate vector stores for entities and hyperedges.
No. Items are ordered by cosine similarity (scores only break ties) and cut at 4,000 tokens per list.

glance.q: Is memory reconstructed at question time?
glance.a: Only by one-hop expansion: entities bring their hyperedges, hyperedges bring their entities, and both bring source chunks.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: Three CSV tables (entities, hyperedges, chunks) inside a fixed prompt asking for reasoning and then an answer; about 9.2k tokens at k = 60 on Medicine.

Each hit brings its graph neighbours and source chunks, and the merged entity, hyperedge and chunk tables go to the generator.

components.role: Embeds entities, hyperedges, chunks and queries

discussion.takeaway: Storing facts as sentences linked to all their entities, rather than as binary triples, and retrieving them together with their source chunks gives the best F1 on the authors' five domain QA sets, where binary graph RAG methods mostly fall below chunk RAG.

claims.claim: HyperGraphRAG beats every baseline in every domain.
claims.evidence: Overall F1 35.35 / 33.89 / 31.30 / 43.81 / 48.71 vs StandardRAG 27.90 / 27.43 / 28.93 / 37.34 / 43.20 (Medicine / Agriculture / CS / Legal / Mix); R-S and G-E also highest. Table 2, §5.2

claims.claim: Binary-relation graph RAG methods often do worse than chunk RAG.
claims.evidence: Medicine overall F1: GraphRAG 17.60, LightRAG 12.79, PathRAG 14.94, HippoRAG2 21.34 vs StandardRAG 27.90. Table 2

claims.claim: Entity retrieval, hyperedge retrieval and chunks each help.
claims.evidence: Medicine F1 35.4 full; 29.8 without entities, 26.4 without hyperedges, 29.2 without chunks, 12.9 with none. Fig. 4, §5.3

claims.claim: The hypergraph captures more knowledge than binary graphs.
claims.evidence: CS: 26,902 hyperedges vs 930 GraphRAG communities and 5,632 LightRAG relations. Fig. 5f, §5.4

claims.claim: Cost stays close to other graph RAG methods.
claims.evidence: 3.084 s and $0.0063 per 1k construction tokens (HippoRAG2 2.758 s / $0.0056); 0.256 s and $3.184 per 1k queries (LightRAG 0.359 s / $3.359). Table 3, §5.7

limits: Text only; images, tables and structured records are left for a multimodal version.
Retrieval uses fixed similarity metrics that may not match downstream usefulness; learning retrieval with RL is future work.
Assumes the knowledge can be centralised; a federated, privacy-preserving version is future work.
A hypergraph is built per task or domain; a pretrained hypergraph retrieval model is future work.
Not yet tested on harder tasks such as multi-hop QA or broader domains.
discussion.limits_src: paper App. I (Limitations and Future Work)
reading: The headline gains over StandardRAG (+7.45 F1, +7.62 R-S, +3.69 G-E) are exactly the Medicine differences in Table 2; averaged over the five domains the gaps are +5.65 F1, +13.1 R-S and +2.67 G-E. The N-ary claim (+5.3 F1) matches the five-domain average, but the Binary claim (+8.6) matches neither (average +5.99, Medicine +9.58).

In the released evaluation code the StandardRAG context is the 'Sources' part of HyperGraphRAG's own retrieval (chunks reached through retrieved entities and hyperedges), not an independent top-5 dense search as App. G states. Its Medicine row (27.90 / 62.57 / 55.66) equals the ablation 'w/o ER & HR' (27.9 / 62.6 / 55.7), consistent with that.

So the StandardRAG gap measures adding the entity and hyperedge tables on top of the same chunks, and the ablation 'without chunks' keeps entity and hyperedge tables whose selection still depends on the graph.
The paper's score weighting (similarity x score with thresholds 50 and 5) and chunk retrieval (k = 5, tau = 0.5) are not in the code; the code uses cosine > 0.2, top 60 and 4,000-token caps per list.
At query time the question is run through the corpus extraction prompt, so hyperedge search matches LLM-written sentences about the question rather than the question itself.

The evaluation sets are built by the authors (GPT-written questions from sampled knowledge fragments, human-checked; 512 per domain); no public QA benchmark is used, although App. I lists multi-hop QA as future work.

G-E averages the judge's seven 0-10 scores with the answer's F1 (App. E Eq. 45), so it is not independent of F1; R-S compares retrieved text with the gold fragments via SimCSE and is 0 for any method that retrieves nothing.

HippoRAG2 is run with 'top-60' units (Table 4) and scores far lower here than in its own paper's setting (for example R-S 18.58 on Agriculture); how its passages were limited to the shared token budget is not described.

abstract.text: HyperGraphRAG argues that graph-based RAG is held back by binary edges, which split facts involving several entities into disconnected triples. It instead has an LLM rewrite documents into short fact sentences, each a hyperedge joining all the entities it involves, stores them as a bipartite graph with vector indexes for entities and hyperedges, and retrieves both before expanding to neighbours and source chunks. On question sets the authors built over medicine, agriculture, computer science, law and a mixed corpus, it reports higher answer F1, retrieval similarity and judged generation quality than chunk RAG and four binary graph RAG methods, at similar cost.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.
